body.p: Pseudorandom functions (PRFs) and their cousins, pseudorandom permutations (PRPs), figure as central tools in the design of protocols, especially those for shared-key cryptography. At one level, PRFs and PRPs can be used to model blockciphers, and they thereby enable the security analysis of protocols based on blockciphers. But PRFs and PRPs are also a useful conceptual starting point in contexts where blockciphers don’t quite fit the bill because of their fixed block-length. So in this chapter we will introduce PRFs and PRPs and investigate their basic properties.

sec.title: 4.1 Function families
sec.p: A function family is a map F: K × D → R. Here K is the set of keys of F, D is the domain of F, and R is the range of F. The set of keys and the range are finite, and all of the sets are nonempty. The two-input function F takes a key K and an input X to return a point Y we denote by F(K, X). For any key K ∈ K we define the map FK: D → R by FK(X) = F(K, X). We call the function FK an instance of function family F. Thus F specifies a collection of maps, one for each key. That’s why we call F a function family or family of functions.
Sometimes we write Keys(F) for K, Dom(F) for D, and Range(F) for R.
Usually K = {0,1}k for some integer k, the key length. Often D = {0,1}ℓ for some integer ℓ called the input length, and R = {0,1}L for some integer L called the output length.

There is some probability distribution on the (finite) set of keys K. Unless otherwise indicated, this distribution will be the uniform one. We denote by K ←$ K the operation of selecting a random string from K and naming it K. We denote by f ←$ F the operation: K ←$ K; f ← FK. In other words, let f be the function FK where K is a randomly chosen key.

A permutation is a bijection (i.e. a one-to-one onto map) whose domain and range are the same set. We say that F is a family of permutations if Dom(F) = Range(F) and each FK is a permutation on this common set.

Example 4.1 A blockcipher is a family of permutations. In particular DES is a family of permutations DES: K × D → R with K = {0,1}56 and D = {0,1}64 and R = {0,1}64. Similarly AES128 is a family of permutations AES: K × D → R with K = {0,1}128 and D = {0,1}128 and R = {0,1}128.

sec.title: 4.2 Random functions and permutations
sec.p: Let D, R ⊆ {0,1}∗ be finite nonempty sets and let ℓ, L ≥ 1 be integers. There are two particular function families that we will often consider. One is Func(D, R), the family of all functions of D to R. The other is Perm(D), the family of all permutations on D. For compactness of notation we let Func(ℓ, L), Func(ℓ), and Perm(ℓ) denote Func(D, R), Func(D, D), and Perm(D), respectively, where D = {0,1}ℓ and R = {0,1}L.

sec.title: 4.2.1 Random functions
sec.p: The family Func(D, R) has domain D and range R. The set of instances of Func(D, R) is the set of all functions mapping D to R. The key describing any particular instance function is simply a description of this instance function in some canonical notation. The key-space of Func(D, R) is the set of all these keys, under the uniform distribution.

For the case of Func(ℓ, L), the key for a function in this family is a list of all output values as its input ranges over {0,1}ℓ. Notice that the key space has size 2L · 2ℓ; there is a key for every function of ℓ-bits to L-bits.
Example 4.2 We exemplify Func(3, 2), meaning ℓ = 3 and L = 2. The domain is {0,1}3 and the range is {0,1}2. An example instance f has input-output table:
The key corresponding to this particular function is (10, 11, 01, 11, 10, 00, 00, 10). The key-space of Func(3, 2) has size 22 · 23 = 216 = 65,536.

A random function g: D → R placed in a black box corresponds to the following: each time you give the box an input, you get back a random element of R, with the sole constraint that if you twice give the box the same input X, it returns the same output g(X). The dynamic view of a random function can be thought of as implemented by a program that maintains a table T, initially empty. On input X: if T[X] is not defined, pick Y ←$ R and set T[X] ← Y; return T[X].

One must remember that the term “random function” is misleading. The randomness of the function refers to the way it was chosen, not to an attribute of the selected function itself. It makes no sense to talk of the randomness of an individual function; the term “random function” just means a function chosen at random.
Example 4.3 Let’s do some simple probabilistic computations to understand random functions. In all of the following, the probability is taken over a random choice of f from Func(ℓ, L).

list-item.p: Fix X ∈ {0,1}ℓ and Y ∈ {0,1}L. Then Pr[f(X) = Y] = 2−L. The probability doesn’t depend on ℓ, nor on the values of X, Y.

Fix X1, X2 ∈ {0,1}ℓ and Y1, Y2 ∈ {0,1}L, and assume X1 ≠ X2. Then Pr[f(X1) = Y1 | f(X2) = Y2] = 2−L. Even if we know the value of f on X1, its value on a different point X2 is equally likely to be any L-bit string.
Fix X1, X2 ∈ {0,1}ℓ and Y ∈ {0,1}L. Then Pr[f(X1) = Y and f(X2) = Y] = 2−2L if X1 ≠ X2, and = 2−L if X1 = X2.
Fix X1, X2 ∈ {0,1}ℓ and Y ∈ {0,1}L. Then Pr[f(X1) ⊕ f(X2) = Y] = 2−L if X1 ≠ X2; 0 if X1 = X2 and Y ≠ 0L; 1 if X1 = X2 and Y = 0L.

Suppose l ≤ L and let τ: {0,1}L → {0,1}l denote the function that returns the first l bits of its input. Fix distinct X1, X2 ∈ {0,1}ℓ, Y1 ∈ {0,1}L and Z2 ∈ {0,1}l. Then Pr[τ(f(X2)) = Z2 | f(X1) = Y1] = 2−l.

sec.title: 4.2.2 Random permutations
sec.p: The family Perm(D) has domain and range D. The set of instances of Perm(D) is the set of all permutations on D. For Perm(ℓ), the key space is the set of all 2ℓ-tuples of distinct ℓ-bit strings, and the key space is equipped with the uniform distribution. Thus π ←$ Perm(ℓ) is the operation of picking a random permutation on {0,1}ℓ.
Example 4.4 We exemplify Perm(3), meaning ℓ = 3. An example instance π has input-output table:
The key-space of Perm(3) has size 8! = 40,320.

In the dynamic view, a random permutation π: D → D placed in a black box corresponds to the following. If you give the box an input X, it returns a point chosen at random from D minus the set of all values previously returned. The dynamic view of a random permutation can be thought of as implemented by a program maintaining a table T, initially empty, and a set S of returned values. On input X: if T[X] is not defined, pick Y ←$ D − S; set T[X] ← Y; S ← S ∪ {T[X]}; return T[X].
Example 4.5 Let’s look at some probabilistic computations involving random permutations. The probability is taken over π ←$ Perm(ℓ).

list-item.p: Fix X, Y ∈ {0,1}ℓ. Then Pr[π(X) = Y] = 2−ℓ. This is the same as if π had been selected from Func(ℓ, ℓ) rather than from Perm(ℓ). The similarity vanishes when more than one point is considered.
Fix X1, X2 ∈ {0,1}ℓ and Y1, Y2 ∈ {0,1}L, and assume X1 ≠ X2. Then Pr[π(X1) = Y1 | π(X2) = Y2] = 1/(2ℓ − 1) if Y1 ≠ Y2, and 0 if Y1 = Y2.
Fix X1, X2 ∈ {0,1}ℓ and Y ∈ {0,1}L. Then Pr[π(X1) = Y and π(X2) = Y] = 0 if X1 ≠ X2, and = 2−ℓ if X1 = X2. This is true because a permutation can never map distinct points to the same point.

sec.title: 4.3 Pseudorandom functions
sec.p: A pseudorandom function is a family of functions with the property that the input-output behavior of a random instance of the family is “computationally indistinguishable” from that of a random function. Someone who has only black-box access to a function has a hard time telling whether the function in question is a random instance of the family or a random function.

We fix a family of functions F: K × D → R. Imagine that you are in a room which contains a terminal connected to a computer outside your room. The computer implements a function g: D → R, so that whenever you type a value X you get back g(X). We consider two different ways in which g will be chosen:
World 0: The function g is drawn at random from Func(D, R), namely g ←$ Func(D, R).
World 1: The function g is drawn at random from F, namely g ←$ F (which means K ←$ K and g is set to FK).

You are not told which of the two worlds was chosen. Your job is to discover which world you are in using only your link enabling you to provide values X and get back g(X). After trying some number of values of your choice, you must output a decision.

In the formalization, the entity referred to as “you” above is an algorithm called the adversary. The adversary algorithm A may be randomized. We formalize the ability to query g as giving A an oracle. We write Ag to mean that adversary A is being given oracle access to function g.
Definition 4.6 Let F: K × D → R be a family of functions, and let A be an algorithm that takes an oracle for a function g: D → R, and returns a bit. We consider two experiments:

disp-quote.p:
Experiment ExpFprf-1(A) Experiment ExpFprf-0(A)
K ←$ K g ←$ Func(D, R)
b ←$ AFK b ←$ Ag
Return b Return b

sec.p: The prf-advantage of A is defined as

The family F is public. The worlds are captured by experiments. The first experiment picks a random instance FK of family F and then runs adversary A with oracle g = FK. The second experiment picks a random function g: D → R and runs A with this oracle. The measure of how well A does at telling the two worlds apart is the prf-advantage of A.

Different adversaries will have different advantages. An adversary may achieve a greater advantage by being more clever in the questions it asks, by asking more questions, or by spending more computing time. The resources of interest include the time-complexity t, the number of queries q, and the total length μ of all queries.

Intuitively, F is “secure” if AdvFprf(A) is “low” for all adversaries whose resources are “practical.” This is our first example of a cryptographic definition. What varies across definitions is the experiments; this is where we pin down how we measure security.

sec.title: 4.4 Pseudorandom permutations
sec.p: A family of functions F: K × D → D is a pseudorandom permutation if the input-output behavior of a random instance of the family is “computationally indistinguishable” from that of a random permutation on D.

When F is a family of permutations, one can consider two settings. One, the adversary gets an oracle for g being tested (chosen-plaintext attack, CPA). The other, the adversary gets, in addition, an oracle for g−1 (chosen-ciphertext attack, CCA).

sec.title: 4.4.1 PRP under CPA
sec.p: We fix a family of functions F: K × D → D. We consider an adversary A with oracle access to a function g chosen in one of two ways: World 0 via g ←$ Perm(D); World 1 via g ←$ F.
Definition 4.7 Let F: K × D → D be a family of functions, and let A be an algorithm that takes an oracle for a function g: D → D, and returns a bit. We consider two experiments:

disp-quote.p:
Experiment ExpFprp-cpa-1(A) Experiment ExpFprp-cpa-0(A)
K ←$ K g ←$ Perm(D)
b ←$ AFK b ←$ Ag
Return b Return b

sec.p: The prp-cpa-advantage of A is defined as

The intuition is similar to that for Definition 4.6. The difference is that here the “ideal” object that F is being compared with is the family of random permutations, not the family of random functions.

sec.title: 4.4.2 PRP under CCA
sec.p: We fix a family of permutations F: K × D → D. We consider an adversary A with oracle access to two functions, g and its inverse g−1.

Definition 4.8 Let F: K × D → D be a family of permutations, and let A be an algorithm that takes an oracle for a function g: D → D and also an oracle for the function g−1: D → D, and returns a bit. We consider two experiments:

disp-quote.p:
Experiment ExpFprp-cca-1(A) Experiment ExpFprp-cca-0(A)
K ←$ K g ←$ Perm(D)
b ←$ AFK, FK−1 b ←$ Ag, g−1
Return b Return b

sec.p: The prp-cca-advantage of A is defined as

The adversary here has more power: not only can it query g, but it can directly query g−1. Informally, a family F is a secure PRP under CCA if AdvFprp-cca(A) is “small” for all adversaries using a “practical” amount of resources.

sec.title: 4.4.3 Relations between the notions
sec.p: If an adversary does not query g−1 the oracle might as well not be there, and the adversary is effectively mounting a chosen-plaintext attack. Thus we have the following:

Proposition 4.9 [PRP-CCA implies PRP-CPA] Let F: K × D → D be a family of permutations and let A be a (PRP-CPA attacking) adversary. Suppose that A runs in time t, asks q queries, and these queries total μ bits. Then there exists a (PRP-CCA attacking) adversary B that runs in time t, asks q chosen-plaintext queries, these queries totaling μ bits, and asks no chosen-ciphertext queries, where AdvFprp-cca(B) ≥ AdvFprp-cpa(A).

The theorem says that if you have an adversary A that breaks F in the PRP-CPA sense, then you have some other adversary B that breaks F in the PRP-CCA sense. As a consequence, PRP-CCA security implies PRP-CPA security.

sec.title: 4.5 Modeling blockciphers
sec.p: One of the primary motivations for the notions of PRFs and PRPs is to model blockciphers and thereby enable the security analysis of protocols that use blockciphers.

Classically, security of blockciphers has focused on key recovery. As we have seen, even a cursory glance at common blockcipher usages shows that hardness of key recovery is not sufficient for security. We suggest that the master security property of a blockcipher is that it be a secure PRP, under either CPA or CCA.

We cannot prove that specific blockciphers have this property. The best we can do is assume they do, and then go on to use them. For quantitative security assessments, we would make specific conjectures about the advantage functions. For example, we might conjecture something like

disp-quote.p: AdvDESprp-cpa(At,q) ≤ c1 · t / TDES / 255 + c2 · q / 240

sec.p: for any adversary At,q that runs in time at most t and asks at most q 64-bit oracle queries. Here TDES is the time to do one DES computation, and c1, c2 are some constants. In other words, we are conjecturing that the best attacks are either exhaustive key search or linear cryptanalysis.
More interesting is AdvDESprf(t, q). Here we cannot do better than assume that
This is due to the birthday attack discussed later. The second term arises because the object under consideration is a family of permutations.

We stress that these are all conjectures. There could exist highly effective attacks that break DES or AES as a PRF without recovering the key. Certainly, to assume that a blockcipher is a PRF is a much stronger assumption than that it is secure against key recovery. Nonetheless, if a blockcipher is broken as a PRF it should be considered insecure, and a replacement should be sought.

sec.title: 4.6 Example attacks
sec.p: Example 4.10 We define a family of functions F: {0,1}k × {0,1}ℓ → {0,1}L as follows. We let k = Lℓ and view a k-bit key K as specifying an L-row by ℓ-column matrix of bits. The input string X = X[1]...X[ℓ] is viewed as a sequence of bits, and F(K, X) is the corresponding matrix-vector product, where all arithmetic is modulo 2.

disp-quote.p:
Adversary Dg
Y ← g(0ℓ)
if Y = 0L then return 1 else return 0

sec.p: We claim that Pr[ExpFprf-1(D) = 1] = 1 and Pr[ExpFprf-0(D) = 1] = 2−L. Why? In Experiment ExpFprf-1(D), g = FK for some K, so g(0ℓ) = 0L and D returns 1. In Experiment ExpFprf-0(D), g is a random function and the probability that g(0ℓ) = 0L is 2−L. Therefore AdvFprf(D) = 1 − 2−L, which is close to 1. Thus F is not a secure PRF.

Example 4.11 Suppose we are given a secure PRF F: {0,1}k × {0,1}ℓ → {0,1}L. We want to use F to design a PRF G: {0,1}k × {0,1}ℓ → {0,1}2L with the same input length but twice the output length. We suggest:
where x̅ denotes the bitwise complement of x. However, G is insecure regardless of the quality of F. The adversary D works as follows:

disp-quote.p:
Adversary Dg
y1 ← g(1ℓ)
y2 ← g(0ℓ)
Parse y1 = y1,1 ‖ y1,2 with |y1,1| = |y1,2| = L
Parse y2 = y2,1 ‖ y2,2 with |y2,1| = |y2,2| = L
if y1,1 = y2,2 then return 1 else return 0

sec.p: Note that 1ℓ is the bitwise complement of 0ℓ. In World 1, GK(1ℓ) = FK(1ℓ) ‖ FK(0ℓ) and GK(0ℓ) = FK(0ℓ) ‖ FK(1ℓ). The first half of y1 always equals the second half of y2, so D returns 1. In World 0, g is a random function, so the probability that the first half of g(1ℓ) equals the second half of g(0ℓ) is 2−L. Therefore AdvGprf(D) = 1 − 2−L, showing G is insecure.

sec.title: 4.7 Security against key recovery
sec.p: Security against key recovery is not sufficient as a notion of security for a blockcipher. However it is certainly necessary. We have indicated that we want to adopt as notion of security for a blockcipher the notion of a PRF or a PRP. If this is to be viable, it should be the case that any function family that is insecure under key recovery is also insecure as a PRF or PRP. In this section we verify this simple fact.
Definition 4.12 Let F: K × D → R be a family of functions, and let B be an algorithm that takes an oracle for a function g: D → R and outputs a string. We consider the experiment:

disp-quote.p:
Experiment ExpFkr(B)
K ←$ Keys(F)
K′ ← BFK
If K′ = K then return 1 else return 0

sec.p: The kr-advantage of B is defined as AdvFkr(B) = Pr[ExpFkr(B) = 1].

Example 4.13 Let F: {0,1}k × {0,1}l → {0,1}L be the family of functions from Example 4.10. The following adversary B recovers the key. Let ej be the l-bit binary string having a 1 in position j and zeros everywhere else.

disp-quote.p:
Adversary BFK
K′ ← ε // ε is the empty string
for j = 1,...,l do
yj ← FK(ej)
K′ ← K′ ‖ yj
return K′

sec.p: The adversary B invokes its oracle to compute the output of the function on input ej. The result yj is exactly the j-th column of the matrix associated to the key K. The matrix entries are concatenated to yield K′, which is returned as the key. Since the adversary always finds the key, AdvFkr(B) = 1.

Proposition 4.14 Let F: K × D → R be a family of functions, and let B be a key-recovery adversary against F. Assume B’s running time is at most t and it makes at most q < |D| oracle queries. Then there exists a PRF adversary A against F such that A has running time at most t plus the time for one computation of F, makes at most q + 1 oracle queries, and
Furthermore if D = R then there also exists a PRP CPA adversary A against F such that A has running time at most t plus the time for one computation of F, makes at most q + 1 oracle queries, and

The Proposition implies that if a family of functions is a secure PRF or PRP then it is also secure against all key-recovery attacks. In particular, if a blockcipher is modeled as a PRP or PRF, we are implicitly assuming it to be secure against key-recovery attacks.

Proof of Proposition 4.14: We prove the first equation. Adversary A is provided an oracle for a function g: D → R, and will try to determine in which World it is. To do so, it runs adversary B as a subroutine.

disp-quote.p:
Adversary Ag
i ← 0
Run adversary B, replying to its oracle queries as follows:
When B makes an oracle query x do
i ← i + 1; xi ← x
yi ← g(xi)
Return yi to B as the answer
Until B stops and outputs a key K′
Let x be some point in D − {x1,...,xq}
y ← g(x)
if F(K′, x) = y then return 1 else return 0

sec.p: A is running B and itself providing answers to B’s oracle queries via the oracle g. When B returns some K′ ∈ K, A tests by checking whether F(K′, x) agrees with g(x) for a new point x not queried by B. We claim that Pr[ExpFprf-1(A) = 1] ≥ AdvFkr(B) and Pr[ExpFprf-0(A) = 1] = 1 / |R|. Subtracting yields Equation (4.1). The first claim is true because in World 1 the oracle g is a random instance of F, which is exactly what B expects. The second is true because in World 0 the function g is random, and since x was never queried by B, the value g(x) is unpredictable. The proof of Equation (4.2) is similar, using the fact that in World 0, g is a random permutation of D and g(x) can assume at least |D| − q values.

Example 4.15 Define the blockcipher E: {0,1}k × {0,1}ℓ → {0,1}ℓ by EK(x) = x for all k-bit keys K and all ℓ-bit inputs x. We claim that it is very secure against key-recovery but very insecure as a PRP under CPA. For any adversary B, AdvEkr(B) = 2−k, regardless of the running time and number of queries made by B. On the other hand there is an adversary A, making only one oracle query, such that AdvEprp-cpa(A) ≥ 1 − 2−ℓ. Since E does not depend on K, querying the oracle yields no information about K, so the key guess is correct with probability only 2−k. On the other hand, an adversary can test whether g(0ℓ) = 0ℓ and achieve a prp-advantage of 1 − 2−ℓ.

sec.title: 4.8 The birthday attack
sec.p: Suppose E: {0,1}k × {0,1}ℓ → {0,1}ℓ is a family of permutations. If we are given an oracle g: {0,1}ℓ → {0,1}ℓ which is either an instance of E or a random function, there is a simple test to determine which: query the oracle at distinct points x1, x2,..., xq, and get back values y1, y2,..., yq. If g were a permutation, the values must be distinct. If g was a random function, they may or may not be distinct. So, if they are distinct, bet on a permutation.

Roughly, it takes q ≈ √2ℓ queries to get an advantage that is quite close to 1. The reason is the birthday paradox. This tells us that an instance of a blockcipher can be distinguished from a random function based on seeing a number of input-output examples which is approximately 2ℓ/2.
Proposition 4.16 Let E: {0,1}k × {0,1}ℓ → {0,1}ℓ be a family of permutations. Suppose q satisfies 2 ≤ q ≤ 2(ℓ+1)/2. Then there is an adversary A, making q oracle queries, such that

Proof of Proposition 4.16: Adversary A queries its oracle g at the first q points in lexicographic order, getting back values y1,...,yq. If all yi are distinct, it returns 1 (betting on a permutation); otherwise it returns 0. In World 1, g = EK for some key K, and since E is a family of permutations, g is a permutation, so y1,...,yq are always all distinct, and A returns 1 with probability 1. In World 0, g is a random function, so y1,...,yq are random independently distributed values in {0,1}ℓ. The probability that they are all distinct is 1 − C(N, q) where N = 2ℓ and C(N, q) is the birthday collision probability. Subtracting gives AdvEprf(A) = C(N, q) ≥ 0.3 · q(q − 1) / 2ℓ.

sec.title: 4.9 The PRP/PRF switching lemma
sec.p: When we analyse blockcipher-based constructions, we find a curious dichotomy: PRPs are what most naturally model blockciphers, but analyses are often considerably simpler and more natural assuming the blockcipher is a PRF. To bridge the gap, we relate the prp-security of a blockcipher to its prf-security. The following says, roughly, these two measures are always close.
Lemma 4.17 [PRP/PRF Switching Lemma] Let E: K × {0,1}n → {0,1}n be a function family. Let A be an adversary that asks at most q oracle queries. Then
As a consequence,

The proof introduces a technique that we shall use repeatedly: a game-playing argument. We are trying to compare what happens when an adversary A interacts with a random permutation oracle to what happens when the adversary interacts with a random function oracle. We set up each of these two interactions as a kind of game, writing out the game in pseudocode. Any time that the behavior in the two games differs, we set a flag bad. The probability that the flag bad gets set is then used to bound the difference between the experiments.

Proof: We prove Equation (4.8), from which Equation (4.9) follows. We define two games, P and R, with pseudocode as follows. In both games, when adversary A asks query X: choose Y ←$ {0,1}n. In Game P (only), if Y is already in Range(π), set bad ← true and re-choose Y from the co-range of π. In both games, set π(X) ← Y and return Y.

Game R perfectly simulates a random function ρ ←$ Func(n): on each query a random n-bit string is returned. Game P simulates a random permutation π ←$ Perm(n): each response is a random new answer, never previously returned. Therefore Pr[Aρ ⇒ 1] = Pr[AGame R ⇒ 1] and Pr[Aπ ⇒ 1] = Pr[AGame P ⇒ 1].

Now: Pr[AGame R ⇒ 1] − Pr[AGame P ⇒ 1] ≤ Pr[AGame R sets bad]. This follows from the fact that any sequence of coin tosses that contributes to the adversary’s advantage (outputting 1 in R and 0 in P) must result in bad being set; otherwise the games produce the same responses and hence the same output.

To bound Pr[AGame R sets bad]: line 11 (the bad-setting line) is executed q times. The first time, Range(π) has 0 points; the second time, 1 point; and so on. Each time, we select a random Y from {0,1}n. By the sum bound, the probability that Y is ever in Range(π) is at most (0 + 1 + 2 + ... + (q − 1)) / 2n = q(q − 1) / 2n+1. This proves Equation (4.8).
The PRP/PRF switching lemma is one of the central tools for understanding block-cipher based protocols, and the game-playing method will be one of our central techniques for doing proofs.

sec.title: 4.10 Unix one-way function
sec.p: The framework for the Unix password-hashing scheme is this. We fix some function h: {0,1}k → {0,1}L, which we call the password hashing function. A user U chooses a k-bit password K, and the system stores the value y = h(K) together with the user’s name U. When the user logs in, the system computes h(K) and declares the user authentic if and only if this value equals y. A party who obtains (U, y) cannot gain trivial entry: they must still find a K such that h(K) = y.

A simple example choice of h is h(K) = DESK(064), so k = 56 and L = 64. To prove anything meaningful, we must make some assumption about DES. We make the assumption that DES is a secure PRP and ask what we can prove about the security of the simplified password scheme.

We need to decide exactly what security property to target. One would think the security question boils down to asking how hard it is to recover K given y = h(K). But recovering any K′ such that h(K′) = y, even if K′ ≠ K, would also break the scheme. This corresponds to asking that h be a one-way function: it is computationally infeasible to recover the pre-image of a range point.
Definition 4.18 Let h: {0,1}k → {0,1}L be a function, and let I be an algorithm that on input an L-bit string returns a k-bit string. We consider the experiment:

disp-quote.p:
Experiment Exphowf(I)
K ←$ {0,1}k; y ← h(K)
x ← I(y)
If h(x) = y then return 1 else return 0

sec.p: The owf-advantage of I is defined as Advhowf(I) = Pr[Exphowf(I) = 1].
Theorem 4.19 Let F: {0,1}k × {0,1}l → {0,1}L be a family of functions, and define h: {0,1}k → {0,1}L via h(K) = F(K, 0l) for all K ∈ {0,1}k. Then we have
under the assumption that k ≤ L − 1. Here t′ is t plus the time for one computation of F.

As per the theorem, Advhowf(t) can be at most twice AdvFprf(t′, 1, l), since k ≤ L − 1 implies 1 / (1 − 2k−L) ≤ 2. So if F is secure, h is also secure. It is thus a proof of security, showing that h is one-way if F is a secure PRF.
Proof of Theorem 4.19: We associate to any adversary I attempting to invert h an adversary DI attacking F such that
This adversary takes an oracle for a function g: {0,1}l → {0,1}L and works as follows:

disp-quote.p:
Adversary DIg
y ← g(0l)
x ← I(y)
If F(x, 0l) = y then return 1 else return 0

sec.p: We claim that Pr[ExpFprf-1(DI) = 1] = Advhowf(I) and Pr[ExpFprf-0(DI) = 1] ≤ 2k / 2L · Advhowf(I). Subtracting and rearranging yields Equation (4.18). Setting ε = Advhowf(I) and dividing both sides by (1 − 2k−L) gives the result.

sec.title: 4.11 Historical notes
sec.p: The concept of pseudorandom functions is due to Goldreich, Goldwasser and Micali, while that of pseudorandom permutation is due to Luby and Rackoff. These works are however in the complexity-theoretic or “asymptotic” setting. In contrast our approach is motivated by the desire to model blockciphers and is called the “concrete security” approach. Definitions 4.6 and 4.7 are from Bellare, Kilian and Rogaway, as are Propositions 4.16 and 4.17.

sec.title: 4.12 Problems
sec.p: Problem 4.1 Let E: {0,1}k × {0,1}n → {0,1}n be a secure PRP. Consider the family of permutations E′: {0,1}k × {0,1}2n → {0,1}2n defined by E′K(x ‖ x′) = EK(x) ‖ EK(x ⊕ x′). Show that E′ is not a secure PRP.

Problem 4.2 Consider the following blockcipher E: {0,1}3 × {0,1}2 → {0,1}2 with eight keys (rows) and the table showing where each of 0, 1, 2, 3 maps. Compute the maximal prp-advantage an adversary can get (a) with one query, (b) with four queries, and (c) with two queries.

Problem 4.3 Present a secure construction for the problem of Example 4.11. That is, given a PRF F: {0,1}k × {0,1}n → {0,1}n, construct a PRF G: {0,1}k × {0,1}n → {0,1}2n which is a secure PRF as long as F is secure.

Problem 4.4 Design a blockcipher E: {0,1}k × {0,1}128 → {0,1}128 that is secure (up to a large number of queries) against non-adaptive adversaries, but is completely insecure (even for two queries) against an adaptive adversary.

Problem 4.5 Let a[i] denote the i-th bit of a binary string a, where 1 ≤ i ≤ |a|. The inner product of n-bit binary strings a, b is ⟨a, b⟩ = a[1]b[1] ⊕ a[2]b[2] ⊕ ··· ⊕ a[n]b[n]. A family of functions F: {0,1}k × {0,1}ℓ → {0,1}L is said to be inner-product preserving if for every K ∈ {0,1}k and every distinct x1, x2 ∈ {0,1}ℓ − {0ℓ} we have ⟨F(K, x1), F(K, x2)⟩ = ⟨x1, x2⟩. Prove that if F is inner-product preserving then there exists an adversary A, making at most two oracle queries, such that AdvFprf(A) ≥ 1/2 · (1 + 1/2L). Explain why this shows that if F is inner-product preserving then F is not a secure PRF.

Problem 4.6 Let E: {0,1}k × {0,1}ℓ → {0,1}ℓ be a blockcipher. The two-fold cascade of E is the blockcipher E(2): {0,1}2k × {0,1}ℓ → {0,1}ℓ defined by E(2)K1 ‖ K2(x) = EK1(EK2(x)). Prove that if E is a secure PRP then so is E(2).

Problem 4.7 Let A be an adversary that makes at most q total queries to its two oracles, f and g, where f, g: {0,1}n → {0,1}n. Assume that A never asks the same query X to both of its oracles. Define Adv(A) = Pr[π ← Perm(n): Aπ(·), π(·) = 1] − Pr[π, π′ ← Perm(n): Aπ(·), π′(·) = 1]. Prove a good upper bound for Adv(A), say Adv(A) ≤ q2 / 2n.

Problem 4.8 Let F: {0,1}k × {0,1}ℓ → {0,1}ℓ be a family of functions and r ≥ 1 an integer. The r-round Feistel cipher associated to F is the family of permutations F(r): {0,1}rk × {0,1}2ℓ → {0,1}2ℓ. (a) Prove that there exists an adversary A, making at most two oracle queries, such that AdvF(2)prf(A) ≥ 1 − 2−ℓ. (b) Prove that there exists an adversary A, making at most two queries to its first oracle and one to its second oracle, such that AdvF(3)prp-cca(A) ≥ 1 − 3 · 2−ℓ.

Problem 4.9 Let E: K × {0,1}n → {0,1}n be a function family and let A be an adversary that asks at most q queries. In trying to construct a proof that |AdvEprp(A) − AdvEprf(A)| ≤ q2 / 2n+1, Michael and Peter put forward an argument a fragment of which is as follows: “Consider an adversary A that asks at most q oracle queries to a function ρ, where ρ is determined by randomly sampling from Func(n). Let C (for ‘collision’) be the event that A asks some two distinct queries X and X′ and the oracle returns the same answer. Then clearly Pr[π ←$ Perm(n): Aπ ⇒ 1] = Pr[ρ ←$ Func(n): Aρ ⇒ 1 | C].” Show that Michael and Peter have it all wrong: prove that Pr[π ←$ Perm(n): Aπ ⇒ 1] is not necessarily the same as Pr[ρ ←$ Func(n): Aρ ⇒ 1 | C]. Do this by selecting a number n and constructing an adversary A for which the left and right sides of the equation above are unequal.
